stances.claim: The 24-month rule of Constitution Art. VIII Sec. 15 is not as clear as it appears, because the period starts only 'from the date of submission,' meaning 'upon receipt by the Court of the memoranda of the parties' -- a definition that is simple with two parties but complex with multiparty cases like Republic v. Lucio Tan, where one petitioner faces at least 27 respondents and not all have filed memos.

The SC has not penalized itself or any of its members for failing to comply with the 24-month deadline, in contrast to RTC judges who 'are penalized at times by separation from service' -- an asymmetry between trial-court and supreme-court accountability that Estelito Mendoza's complaint surfaces.

In multiparty cases like Republic v. Tan, where some respondents' counsel 'moved' offices and another respondent 'was not residing at given address,' the Court has procedural cover for non-decision -- but CJ's proposed fix is to deem the case submitted on the date the Court ordered memoranda filed (over four years ago), treat non-filing parties as having waived their right, and penalize their lawyers for failure to comply.

When new appointees 'inherit' cases from retired predecessors -- receiving 'unloaded' old cases to reach the incumbent average -- the question whether the 24-month clock begins on the assignment date or on the original memo-receipt date is genuinely open; CJ's view is that the Court and the retired justice may have violated the limit but the new justice has not.
stances.rhetorical_move: clock-attribution clarification (protect successors from inherited blame)

stances.claim: Beyond the constitutional requirements of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' justices and judges must also be 'industrious and diligent' -- endorsing reader Luis M. Ermitano's RTC critique that most judges don't start on time, don't exhaust calendared cases, and don't fully use stipulations of facts, mediation, or pretrial proceedings.

notable_anecdotes: The 'hackles raised' framing -- CJ's two prior columns produced strong pushback 'especially in the legal community,' converting reader anger into the column's opening occasion.

Estelito P. Mendoza characterized as 'abogado de campanilla' (bell-class lawyer) -- the elite-bar respect title placed alongside his complaint, which makes the pushback higher-stakes than ordinary reader correspondence.

The Republic v. Tan multiparty arithmetic -- 'one petitioner' against 'at least 27 respondents,' with Tan, Carmen Tan, and several controlled companies represented by Mendoza filing memos 'more than four years ago,' while other respondents (with lawyers who 'moved' or who were 'not residing at given address') still have not -- physicalizing why the 24-month rule under-determines outcomes in complex litigation.

CJ's uncharacteristic register-break -- 'the case Mendoza is so pissed about' -- a rare colloquial flash in an otherwise doctrinal column, marking CJ's amused acknowledgment of the great lawyer's annoyance.

The inherited-cases mechanics -- new appointees with under-average inherited dockets get more old cases 'unloaded' to them by incumbents to equalize the average, while those above the average retain all theirs -- exposing the SC's internal load-balancing pragmatics few outsiders see.
The closing space-acknowledgment -- 'Sorry, I have no more space for other equally important reactions' -- CJ's regular nod to the column-format constraint and the volume of reader correspondence.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to the pushback his two prior columns on judicial delays -- 'Confronting SC's mounting backlog' (April 7, 2019) and 'Will judges-at-large solve huge RTC backlog?' (April 14, 2019) -- provoked in the legal community. Leading the pack is 'abogado de campanilla' Estelito P. Mendoza, who complains that he has several SC cases unresolved beyond the 24-month constitutional deadline (Art. VIII Sec. 15) -- particularly Republic v. Lucio C. Tan, et al. (G.R. 203592) -- and asks what consequences attach to the Court's own violation, given that RTC judges 'are penalized at times by separation from service.' CJ answers directly that the SC has not penalized itself or its members. He then explains the definitional complication: the 24 months start from 'date of submission,' meaning receipt of the parties' memoranda -- easy with two parties but unclear with the 27-respondent Republic v. Tan, where Tan, his wife Carmen, and Mendoza-represented controlled companies filed memos 'more than four years ago' while the remaining respondents have not. A February 20, 2018 SC resolution noted that 2017 orders 'could not be served on some respondents' because their lawyers 'moved' and one respondent 'was not residing at given address.' Without commenting on the merits, CJ proposes that the case be deemed submitted on the date the Court ordered memos filed (over four years ago), with non-filing parties waiving their right and their lawyers penalized for failure to comply. He raises a second structural difficulty: new SC appointees 'inherit' cases from retired predecessors and may be 'unloaded' with old cases by incumbents to equalize the per-justice average -- leaving open whether the 24 months begin on assignment date or original memo-receipt date. His view is that 'the Court (and the retired justice) may have violated the 24-month limit, the new justice has not.' Finally, he endorses lawyer Luis M. Ermitano's complementary critique of RTC judges who 'do not start on time,' do not take up calendared cases, and do not fully use stipulations of facts, mediation, or pretrial proceedings -- agreeing that beyond the constitutional requirements of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' justices and judges must also be 'industrious and diligent.' He closes by acknowledging the column-space constraint: 'Sorry, I have no more space for other equally important reactions.'
